title: Jackson County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Jackson County wells have a 100 ft median depth. Review reported yields, water levels, drilling costs and checks before buying rural land.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Jackson County
intro_html:
A well budget in Jackson County starts with a relatively modest median depth: 100 feet. But depth alone does not tell you how dependable the water supply will be. Fractured mountain ground can produce very different results on neighboring properties.

Colorado DWR records include 1,600 permitted wells countywide, with 1,142 recorded as constructed. Use these records to narrow your questions before buying around Walden or elsewhere in the county—not as a promise of what a new hole will produce.

sections.heading: A 100-Foot Median, With Room for a Deeper Hole
sections.html:
Among the 1,180 Jackson County wells reporting depth, the median is 100 feet, and the middle half falls between 60 and 160 feet. That is a useful starting range for discussing a drilling bid, not a depth guarantee. The 90th-percentile depth is 258 feet, so a budget based only on the median can leave you short.

The permit data group 1,577 wells under unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers; only small numbers specifically name Alluvial or Coalmont. In fractured mountain bedrock, usable water depends on the fractures a borehole intersects. Compare nearby completion reports around your parcel, especially where terrain changes, rather than carrying a depth assumption across the county.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Usually Support Household Planning
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gpm, with the middle half between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm. Those figures give a buyer a reasonable starting point for household supply planning, but only 260 wells report yield. They do not describe every permitted well in Jackson County.

Of the reported yields, 2% are under 1 gpm and 9% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. A low-producing well may need storage and careful demand management. Even a stronger recorded yield is not a current performance guarantee. Before closing, have the well's sustained production and recovery evaluated, and confirm that the permit authorizes your intended water use.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Countywide Drop
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to resting water, not the bottom of the well. Jackson County's median is 30 feet below ground, with the middle half between 13 and 60 feet. Only 83 wells report this measurement, so the county summary is a limited guide to conditions at a particular property.

Median measurements were 32 feet in the 2000s, 50 feet in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. That sequence does not show a steady decline. It also does not establish recovery at an individual well because the summaries may represent different wells. Ask for repeat measurements and pumping observations from the well you are buying.

sections.heading: Jackson County's Permit History and Drilling Names
sections.html:
The largest listed decade for permits was the 1990s, with 374, followed by 272 in the 2000s. Records show 142 in the 2010s and 96 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, and permit issuance does not establish when—or whether—a well was constructed.

Stolns & Son Drilling (Stolns, Lewis B.) appears on 213 records, and James Drilling (Keaton, Jordan K.) on 56. Another frequent entry, “Authorized (Pe, Pg),” appears on 95; verify the actual drilling contractor behind that label. Historical record counts are useful for finding local experience, but they do not establish present availability or licensing.

sections.heading: Budget for the Finished Well, Not Just Drilling
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock such as granite or gneiss, the supplied Jackson County cost model uses $65–$100 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $6,500–$10,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $12,500–$22,000.

Use that finished-well range as an initial planning allowance, not a parcel-specific quote. Ask the driller to spell out casing, grout, mobilization, testing and the treatment of additional footage. Rig access and the route from the well to the house also matter. A bid should make clear what happens financially if drilling must continue or the hole fails to produce usable water.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Site Constraints Before Closing
sections.html:
The environmental map identifies 28 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 54 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles in the supplied search. These are screening flags, not evidence that a particular Jackson County well is contaminated. Check each site's location, status and relationship to the parcel, then select laboratory testing with qualified local guidance.

Also inspect the wellhead, casing condition and drainage, and review septic placement and records. A yield entry cannot rule out a future shortage, and the supplied records do not establish dry-hole odds. For a building lot, resolve well access, septic suitability and the house location together before committing to a layout.

sections.heading: Buying Near Walden: Start With the Parcel's Records
sections.html:
Start with the actual permit and completion report, then compare neighboring wells. Walden has its own local page, while Routt County and Grand County provide nearby regional context. Neither a county boundary nor a nearby address guarantees comparable underground conditions.

Domestic/household use accounts for 68% of Jackson County permit records and stock use for 23%, but those categories do not grant rights to a different parcel. Ask DWR to confirm the proposed household, livestock or outdoor uses. For an existing home, obtain a current production evaluation and water-quality results. For vacant land, get drilling and site-development input before treating the lot as ready to build.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Jackson County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 100 feet, and the middle half of wells falls between 60 and 160 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 258 feet. Those figures come from 1,180 depth records countywide. Nearby completion reports are more useful for a parcel-specific estimate because fractured-bedrock conditions can change over short distances.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Jackson County?
faq.a: The supplied model estimates $65–$100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the county's 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $6,500–$10,000, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $12,500–$22,000. Get a written scope covering casing, grout, access and additional drilling before relying on that budget.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Jackson County?
faq.a: Among 260 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gpm and the middle half is 7.0–15.0 gpm. Reported yields under 1 gpm account for 2%. These are historical measurements, not promises of current output. Have the property's well evaluated for sustained production and recovery before planning household demand or storage.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Jackson County?
faq.a: The supplied facts do not establish drinking-water safety for any individual well. The environmental search lists 28 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 54 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Their presence does not prove contamination at your property. Review nearby site information and obtain laboratory testing tailored to the well and local concerns.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Jackson County?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a steady drop: water was 32 feet below ground in the 2000s, 50 feet in the 2010s and 30 feet in the 2020s. Only 83 wells report static levels, and these are not necessarily repeated measurements of the same wells. Check the property's own measurement history for a meaningful local trend.
